1:
The title is read as covering everything that follows. Gill takes it for the general title of the whole book, and insists the words are not the prophet's own but the Lord's put into his mouth, the Greek and Arabic versions saying so outright by rendering it the word of God. Henry works the genealogy: this Hilkiah is supposed not to be the high priest of the day, who would have been named as such rather than as one of the priests in Anathoth. The name means one raised up by the Lord, and Henry notes the man was already authorized to teach as a priest, the extraordinary commission being added to that; as with the priest who prophesied among the captives, God was supporting an order then sadly eclipsed.

Anathoth is placed alike by three: Henry about three miles from Jerusalem, a city of priests where a high priest of the older time had his country house; Wesley at the same distance, allotted to the priests out of Benjamin; Clarke a village of that tribe within a few miles of the city, appointed for the descendants of Aaron.

What the times were like divides the emphasis. Keil and Delitzsch describe unbroken peace: Assyria had been crushed before the gates of Jerusalem in the earlier reign, the Medes had asserted independence, Babylon had risen in insurrection, and though one energetic successor propped the tottering throne for a time, his heirs could not. Calvin looks at the same years and sees the opposite: religion wholly vitiated because the Book of the Law had been lost, impiety prevailing by long custom, and the heaviest burden laid on a man bringing the people back to a doctrine most were treading underfoot. Henry ties the call to the throne: the king had begun his reformation the year before, and a young prophet was seasonably raised up to assist and encourage a young king. Ellicott presses the same coincidence, dates the king at twenty or twenty-one with his active reformation five years later, and counts eighteen years of ministry under that reign.

How young the prophet was is the one flat contradiction. Clarke puts him at probably fourteen. Calvin calls that conjecture frivolous and argues from the word, which does not properly mean a child but a youth or a young man, as it is used of a patriarch's trained servants and of the attendant at the tabernacle. Ellicott assumes about twenty and works forward: the prophet would then have been sixty or sixty-one at the captivity.

The span they agree on and count differently. Wesley gives forty-one years in Judea besides the time in Egypt, and observes that eighteen fell under the first reign. Clarke gives upwards of forty and carries it past the fall of the city, the prophet dying in Egypt two years after. On the reigns passed over, Ellicott notes that two of three months each are omitted for the more conspicuous reigns of eleven years apiece; Gill accounts for one by its brevity and suggests perhaps no word of the Lord came in that time.

Clarke alone sketches the man: called very young, he tried to excuse himself on the ground of youth and incapacity, was overruled by the divine authority, and then reproved a perverse people at the hazard of his life; he might have made terms with the enemy and gained ease and plenty, and chose to stay and take his part in the disasters. Calvin alone raises a chronological doubt at the succession: since the father began to reign at twenty-two and reigned only two years, and the son came to the throne at eight, the son must have been begotten in his father's fifteenth year, which is not likely, so probably a son by law rather than by nature, as a later king is called son though many think him a nephew.
4:
What kind of event the coming of the word was they fill in differently. Clarke has him first feel the inspiring influence of the Spirit, which gave the subjects and the words alike. Ellicott reasons from the silence: revelation often came with the tension of a trance, a dream or an open vision, and almost presupposed a training inward or outward; since none of that appears here, we must assume a distinct consciousness that the voice in his inmost soul was from Jehovah.

On being known before birth they converge. Gill distinguishes it from bare omniscience: this is knowledge with special love joined to it, older than the foundation of the world. Ellicott gets the same from the Hebrew, where the word implies not foreknowledge only but choice and approval. Clarke says the plan was formed and the envoy appointed before birth, as the apostle speaks of his own call. Wesley reads sanctified as ordained to a public service, said to this prophet and not the others because he needed more encouragement in his tender years.

Prophet to the nations is Ellicott's largest claim, the distinguishing characteristic of the work: other prophets were sent to Israel and Judah with occasional parentheses touching the Gentiles, while this horizon extended more widely, in part to make them drink the cup of fury and in part to witness a brighter future, as though he had drunk in the spirit of the prophet who spoke of a light to the Gentiles. Henry hears the phrase as to or against, and puts the Jews first among the nations, since they had learned their works and would not otherwise be numbered with them; and keeps the office open, the prophet still telling nations what judgments follow national sins.

What the excuse means splits the two grammarians outright. Keil and Delitzsch insist the words are not what Moses said: Moses lacked the gift of utterance, was not a man of words, whereas this man only thinks himself unequal to the task through youth and inexperience. Ellicott renders the very same clause as what Moses said, a man of words, having no gifts of utterance. On the age he is careful: later Jewish writers fix fourteen as the limit of the term, but here it is more indefinite, a man conscious of his weakness naturally using a word below his actual standing, so any age up to twenty-one may be assumed. Gill takes the exclamation from the Jewish commentators as a word of distress and grief, the prophet uneasy at his call.

Why he refused is Calvin's question, and he gives two answers. The refusal clears him of any suspicion of rashness, since many wish to be teachers and hardly one is not anxious to be heard, and it gains him esteem and makes his hearers attentive. What frightened him was the difficulty, and God pardoned his servant, since it was not his design to reject the call or shake off the yoke. Clarke turns the shrinking into a test of ministry: those really called know their own weakness, while those never called run for worldly honour.

The answer is short, and they read it alike. Clarke has God say the words are his and not the messenger's, so youth is no hindrance; Wesley makes it a promise of eloquence and courage; Ellicott calls the misgiving not reluctance, God giving the work and the power with it; Keil and Delitzsch add that he was to publish no thoughts of his own but the counsel revealed to him. On the faces, Gill sees stern looks and angry countenances threatening death, Keil and Delitzsch a youthful bashfulness before great personages, and Calvin the deeper cause: a degenerate people who had shaken off the yoke for years and were exulting in their freedom, so that the prophet refused indirectly, never confessing plainly how it stood.
9:
Who stretched out the hand is answered three ways. Gill reports the Jewish reading that it was the Angel who spoke in the Lord's name and is called by his name, and prefers the Son of God, the true Jehovah, in a human form assumed for the occasion. Wesley leaves it open, either the hand of an angel or God himself in some visible shape. Ellicott takes it for something like a waking vision, recalling the live coal laid on the lips of the earlier prophet, and identifies the hand of the Lord as the received symbol of the Spirit's special influence, the act conveying new powers of thought and utterance.

What the touch signified they agree on and prove differently. Keil and Delitzsch argue from the organ: the hand is the instrument of making and doing, so touching the mouth is an emblem that God frames there what the man is to speak, a tangible pledge of inspiration. Ellicott argues from a parallel, that the words a prophet speaks are no more his own than those the apostles were to speak, which were put into their hearts by the Spirit of the Father. Calvin makes it a test: this is how a true call may be ascertained, when a man brings nothing of his own but speaks as the oracles of God, not doubtingly, as though offering his own glosses, so that whatever proceeds from the wit of man is to be disregarded.

What being set over the nations means is held down carefully. Gill says not as a prince but as a prophet, to prophesy things concerning them which would certainly come to pass. Ellicott presses the word to its literal sense, deputy or representative, and divides the objects: the nations are those outside Israel, the kingdoms take it in. Wesley names the empires and keeps the office over whole nations rather than single persons.

The rooting up and building is where an idiom must be explained, and Clarke and Wesley reach it independently in nearly the same words: by scripture usage the prophets are said to do what they foretell shall come to pass, so they rooted up by declaring judgments and built by declaring promises. Clarke sets beside it the command given to the earlier prophet to make the heart of this people fat, which he reads as showing them they are stupid and blind. Where the two part is on the shape of the whole. Wesley reads it conditionally, metaphors from architects and gardeners, either the destroying words for God's enemies and the building for his friends, or rather both on a condition: repent and he will settle them in the land, refuse and he will pull them down. Ellicott reads a sequence in time, the work seeming at first simply destructive, to root out and ruin, to destroy and rend asunder, with the hope of construction beyond it, the whole sequel of the book a comment on these words as it passes through terror and darkness to the new covenant.

Calvin alone asks what the investiture is for. It shows how reverently God would have his word received even when conveyed by frail mortals: there is no one who does not pretend to desire obedience, yet hardly one in a hundred really receives it, some raising a clamour, others evading, others secretly opposing. He also asks what prophets are sent for, and answers that they are to reduce the world to order, not sparing their hearers but reproving them freely and using threatenings where men are perverse. And it arms the prophet, who was to remember his calling and not flatter men servilely or indulge their passions, since teachers cannot firmly execute their office unless they keep the majesty of God before their eyes, the sight of men of any dignity at all bringing fear with it.
11:
The pun is the whole vision, and every voice tries to carry it over. Clarke names it a paronomasia and lays the two words side by side: the almond is the hastening tree, the one that first awakes, and the answer says I will hasten, or watch over, my word for the first opportunity. Ellicott says the play cannot be reproduced, the Hebrew forming a participle from the same root, and renders the sense literally, I too am watching over my word to perform it; he adds that the name used here is the poetical one, not the common name of the tree. Wesley attempts an English equivalent anyway and gets a verb out of it: I will almond-tree it, that is, I will be upon them speedily. Calvin traces the same derivation and declines to render the noun almond at all, the verb behind it meaning to watch or hasten.

Two of them reach for the same naturalist. Henry has the almond among the forwardest trees of the spring, in bud while others are scarcely broken out, flourishing in January and with ripe fruit by March, whence the Hebrew calls it the hasty tree. Clarke quotes the same passage in the original: it blossoms in January when other trees are locked in their winter repose, and bears fruit in March, as the spring begins.

What the branch means divides them cleanly. Henry sees a correcting rod hanging over the people, denoting affliction and chastisement, and Clarke reports the same from a modern commentator: a rod being an instrument of punishment, this is the symbol of the punishment about to be announced. Ellicott reads it in the opposite key. The bough stands in contrast to the words of terror and in harmony with the words of hope, bright pink blossoms and pale green leaves, the token of an early spring rising out of the dreariness of winter; and the haste it signifies is a divine haste that will not delay the fulfilment of a gracious promise, but makes it bud and blossom and bear fruit.

Wesley takes the rod as a portent and dates it. This vision and that of the caldron are thought to have come together; the tree had leaves and probably blossoms, like the rod that budded in the tabernacle; and the sight worked like a comet, showing the miseries at hand, the death of the king which soon followed, the taxing under the king of Egypt, the breaking in of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites, and at last the captivity.

Henry reads the exchange as a lesson in method. Having answered the objection that he was a child, God goes on to initiate him in the prophetical learning and language; having promised to make him speak intelligibly, he now teaches him to understand what is said to him, for prophets must have eyes as well as tongues and be seers as well as speakers. Ellicott notes the symbols were not selected by the prophet, and yet were adapted to his previous training and the bent of his character, their poetry of exquisite beauty.

Calvin objects to a narrow reading. Interpreters, he says, unwisely confine the promise to the punishments mentioned afterwards, as though it meant only that the threatenings would not be without effect. That is too restricted: God is extolling his word as such, not speaking by his servants for their words to vanish into air, but with power accompanying them, as another prophet has it, the word not returning empty but prospering. He therefore reads these verses as confirming what went before rather than opening a new subject, and cites the apostle on true teachers armed with power against the unbelieving. Gill puts it in a line: the thing seen is a proper emblem of what God is about to do, and of the quick dispatch to be made in it.
13:
What the pot is stands open. Clarke reports two constructions and refuses to decide: some make Judea the pot, agitated by the invasion of a people whose land lay north, while a modern scholar renders the clause from the face of the north and makes the pot the northern empire itself, pouring out its multitudes like a thick vapour; either, he says, suits the text. Ellicott and Wesley take the second without hesitation, Ellicott a large cauldron set on a great pile of burning wood and tipped to empty its scalding contents southward, Wesley the Babylonian army besieging the city as a fire plays round a pot. On the face they differ quietly: for Ellicott the mouth turned away from the north, for Wesley the front of the furnace where the fire is blown up.

Ellicott marks the contrast and the escalation. The cauldron was as strong a contrast as possible to the vernal beauty of the almond-bough, and told too plainly what to expect from the regions north of the land; water at the boiling point went beyond the waters of the great river in the older symbolism. Calvin asks instead why the vision comes as question and answer: had it only been said that he saw a boiling pot, with the metaphor explained, the narrative would have less force, but God set forth as present and explaining makes the prediction certain and proves him its author.

One clause yields two words to two readers. Clarke stops at the verb, which means shall be opened: the door is to be thrown abroad that these calamities may pass out freely. Ellicott stops at the noun and makes it definite, the evil, long foretold and long expected.

Who the northern families are they fill out. Gill keeps them within one jurisdiction and adds, from Kimchi, that the calling of them is no other than putting it into their hearts to come. Wesley makes them nations under one lord, the Babylonians and their assistants, the Medes in confederacy. Ellicott reads the Hebrew as apposition, all the families, even the kingdoms of the north, and lets in the Scythians besides, who about this time spread like a deluge over Asia Minor and Syria, on the authority of a Greek historian; he also renders the verb as a present, so that the evil is not merely future but actually begun.

The thrones at the gates split them. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the verse interprets the picture at all, calling it a direct statement of what was to fall on the inhabitants, and read the throne as the seat of sovereignty rather than of judgment, a figure for establishing dominion. Clarke and Ellicott read it judicially: the gates were where justice was administered, so the invaders usurp it, setting up their thrones of judgment where kings had sat to hear complaints, and lay the whole country under their own laws. Wesley takes the plainest sense, seats, pavilions or tents pitched, which shall be as so many thrones.

Against whom the judgments are uttered Calvin raises and answers. Many interpreters, he says, refer them to the Chaldeans, as though God were prescribing what was decreed, as chief judges do to those under them; the exposition is strained, confuted by what follows. Gill settles it in a line, not against the kingdoms of the north but against this people. Keil and Delitzsch add that the phrase is peculiar to this prophet, meaning properly to have a lawsuit with someone, comprehending trial and sentence and not merely remonstrance. Ellicott enumerates the counts, apostasy, the transfer of adoration to other gods, and the worship of graven images, while Clarke makes idolatry the source of the whole and notes that more than a hundred manuscripts read the singular: it was their one great work, the business of their life, their trade.
17:
Four of them explain the girding from the same custom and one from its purpose. Gill takes the loins of mind and body alike, and reads the eastern habit of trussing long garments for quicker dispatch as designing haste in the Lord's work as well as resolution of mind. Clarke gives the robes trussed under the girdle on a journey or at ordinary work, so that the motions of the body might not be impeded; Wesley the same, that they might not hinder where expedition was required; Keil and Delitzsch the garment fastened up to make a man fit for labour, a journey or a race. Ellicott passes over the wardrobe: be as the messenger who prepares to be swift on his errand and to go wherever he is sent, an image of intense activity that reappears in the later scriptures and has become proverbial in the speech of Christendom.

The threat attached to the charge is where Clarke will not rest. Be not dismayed, lest I dismay thee: Ellicott keeps the repetition, which the Hebrew uses for emphasis, and Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way, while Wesley keeps the sting, lest I destroy thee in their sight, to become their reproach. Clarke offers two ways out. Either God is here represented as doing what he only permits or suffers to be done, or the clause should be read as reassurance rather than warning: do not fear that I shall confound thee before them, as a modern commentator renders it.

Ellicott alone reads a temperament out of the repetition. The calls to courage come so often that they seem to indicate a constitutional timidity, as the exhortations in the letters to a young colleague do; and he offers an excuse, that a recent reign had shown how easily the work might end in the martyr's fate, and that even the prophet among the exiles by the river needed the same encouragement.

The three images are unpacked with unusual particularity. Ellicott sees strength heaped upon strength: the man is attacked by kings, princes, priests and people as the cities were by invading armies, but the issue is different, for they fall and he holds out. He identifies the pillar as the one rising in the centre of an eastern house to carry the flat roof and make it a terrace where men may meet, and thinks the brazen walls refer to plates of copper fastened over the brick or stone of a fortification. Clarke keeps it simpler, impregnable as a city, unshaken as a pillar, imperishable as a wall of brass, and adds that the issue proved the promise: the prophet outlived every insult and saw his enemies carried away. Gill notes that four versions read a comparison, as a defenced city, one that cannot be taken; Clarke that many manuscripts read the wall in the singular, matching the singular nouns before it.

Calvin puts the caution the images invite. The man would have invincible power and great trials both, so that his office would not be, as the saying goes, a mere play; he was made a fortified city that he might fight manfully, not so that danger and everything grievous to the flesh should be kept away from him. From this he draws a rule: when God promises his servants victory over their enemies, they are not to make it an occasion of fostering their torpor or idleness, but of gathering courage to proceed boldly and unweariedly in the course of their vocation.

Two closing notes. Wesley takes the whole land as all its inhabitants without distinction, and hears in it that the troubles would be not only great but long, running through several reigns. Clarke reaches for a line of one of the ancients: God protecting thee, though thou wert at sea upon a twig, thou shouldst be safe.
